restatements.text: Requires corporations that spend more than $10,000 in a year on independent political expenditures to publicly disclose the names of individuals who contributed more than $1,000 toward those expenditures.

analysis.answer: Under current law, corporations report the total amount they spend on independent political expenditures but not the sources of those funds. The measure changes this by requiring them to disclose the sources (contributors over $1,000) once their expenditures exceed $10,000.
Direct costs include the administrative expense for corporations to track and report donor information, as well as state expenses to process and publish these disclosures.

Corporations and their donors bear the cost of reduced privacy and increased administrative burden. Voters, journalists, and advocacy groups benefit from increased visibility into who is funding political spending.

Donors seeking privacy may cap their contributions at $1,000 or route their funding through other entities not covered by this exact requirement. Corporations may keep their independent expenditures just under $10,000 to avoid triggering the disclosure rule.

It addresses an information gap regarding the financial backers of corporate political spending. The mechanism requires disclosure of large donors, which provides this information to the public but may also create an incentive to use alternative, undisclosed spending channels.
